strengths: The paper addresses an important question: what multimodal contrastive learning recovers, and whether those representations support disentanglement. Separating coupled semantic variables from modality-specific variation is a useful modeling perspective.

The empirical scope is broad, covering multiple CLIP backbones, few-shot benchmarks, distribution shifts, CelebA traversals, and Multimodal3DIdent. Several reported improvements are substantial; for example, the ViT-B/16 two-shot target average increases from 32.51 to 37.13.

The proposed post-processing is straightforward to implement. Synthetic experiments include repeated runs and violations of distributional assumptions, providing useful evidence about empirical behavior.
weaknesses: The central proof relies on a false optimization claim. Lemma 2 states that the minimum of L−2logN is zero, but zero is achieved by collapsed encoders and informative encoders can do better. Under the paper’s uniform-circle/vMF model with k=1 and temperature 1, identity encoders with dot-product scoring give approximately −0.421. Moreover, condition C1 requires identical embeddings for every positive pair; the full-support noisy conditional makes this imply constant encoders, contradicting uniformity condition C2. Both identifiability proofs use this lemma to establish their essential shared-encoder reduction, so the central guarantees are unsupported.

The convex-body analysis has additional substantive errors. Lemma 3 establishes limiting uniformity as λ approaches zero, but Eq. (43) assumes exact uniformity at finite λ, where boundary-dependent normalization generally makes p(z_t) nonuniform. Corollary 2 also claims permutation identifiability for an arbitrary norm, although Appendix E.2 requires an Lα metric with α≠2. Euclidean distance on a ball admits arbitrary rotations, contradicting the stated permutation-only ambiguity.

The FastICA guarantee is incompatible with the hyperspherical assumptions. Uniform spherical coordinates are dependent and rotationally invariant, so marginal linear ICA cannot identify their original orientation. Having M−1 intrinsic dimensions does not establish independent linearly mixed sources. Appendix O also labels arbitrary orthogonal mixing as component-wise disentanglement, although such mixing generally combines factors. The proposed PCA/local-isometry argument does not supply a rigorous alternative.

The downstream experiments do not isolate disentanglement from ordinary preprocessing. FastICA includes whitening and dimension reduction, and Appendix K compares 300 ICA components against 160 or 200 components in the PCA+ICA pipeline. Matched-dimension PCA/whitening controls are essential. In particular, the orthogonal ICA rotation after whitening leaves an appropriately optimized L2-regularized linear probe unchanged, so classification gains cannot establish that independent axes caused the improvement.

The recovery evaluations do not fully substantiate the claims. Appendix K regresses learned representations on true latents; high R² in this direction does not establish invertible recovery and can conceal lost factors. Multimodal3DIdent provides useful quantitative evidence, but its aggregate linear-recovery scores do not establish component-wise disentanglement or an advantage over matched preprocessing baselines. Selected CelebA traversals likewise do not establish isolated factors.

The 'beyond DAGs' positioning needs stronger justification. An observational joint distribution can be factorized in either direction, while heterogeneous mechanisms can be represented using an explicit regime variable. Replacing a directed relationship with an undirected coupling does not itself establish greater causal expressiveness. The paper needs clearer causal semantics and a precise comparison separating its contribution from existing contrastive-identifiability results.

Reproducibility and reporting remain incomplete: the main downstream results lack uncertainty estimates, the data used to fit PCA/ICA are insufficiently specified, and Appendix P omits important training and evaluation details. There is also a concrete arithmetic error: Table 2’s RN101 baseline target scores average approximately 22.03, rather than the reported 20.03.
